title: Get 38% off an RTX 5070-powered HP Omen 35L gaming desktop sporting an Intel Core Ultra 7 CPU and 32GB of DDR5
summary: TKTK
content: HP's Omen prebuilt PC comes in a standard mid-tower size, but crams in an RTX 5070 GPU, 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory, and an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F. Boasting a steep 38% discount at HP for Black Friday , this system offers mid-range specs at a comfortable mid-range price. One thing to note about HP's modern prebuilt desktops is that, unlike the days of yore, they actually use standardized parts, meaning that upgrading the system later down the line (perhaps when PC component pricing calms down), you'll be all set to upgrade without the hassle of having to work around proprietary boards and parts. Check out the HP Omen 35L gaming desktop at HP US Alongside the CPU GPU, and RAM, you also get a 1TB PCIe Gen 4 drive for all of the games you'll download onto the system, and there's also a spare slot, in case you want to expand the capacity in the future, and whenever the price of RAM comes down, you might also wish to populate the two empty DIMM slots over on the motherboard. OMEN 35L Gaming Desktop (RTX 5070, Core Ultra 7): was $3599.99 now $2199.99 Get an RTX 5070-powered PC, paired with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F, 32GB of Kingston Fury DDR5-6000 RAM, and a 1TB SSD; the system also offers plenty of space to upgrade storage and memory capacities in the future. Expect a solid mid-tower chassis with an 850W power supply and an Intel B860 chipset motherboard. View Deal Intel has not specified the make or manufacturer of the B860 motherboard contained within the system, but we do get further details about its I/O and connectivity options. Expect a Realtek connectivity chipset with support for WI-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3 for all your controllers and peripherals, alongside a host of ports, including 2x USB-C 10Gbps, 4x USB-A ports at 5Gbps, and a further 4x USB-A 2.0 ports. The entire system makes for a solid 1440p-focused build, and with the RTX 5070 paired nicely with Intel's Core Ultra 7 265KF, the 20-core CPU, consisting of 8 P-cores and 12 E-cores, will perform nicely, with boost clocks at up to 5.4GHz on the P-cores. Therefore, our mystery unspecified motherboard will be running LGA 1851, which is running towards its end of life. So, while other aspects of the system remain fairly upgradable, do be aware that if you want a CPU upgrade, drop-in options will be limited without having to switch platforms to Nova Lake or other future architectures. Despite this, you can't refute a good offer, and armed with a staggering $1400 off its current MSRP at HP for Black Friday , it still offers heaps of value in the current climate. content: Hoto's electronic screwdrivers are legendary at Tom's Hardware towers, and now you can get a kit for yourself at 43% off over on Amazon this Black Friday . The kit costs just $28.48 and can be used for several jobs, from electronics repairs to home renovations, and pretty much any other job that requires a screwdriver. Check out the Hoto 25-piece Cordless Screwdriver kit at Amazon This is the latest model from Hoto, and it comes finished in a smart royal blue, made from a tough plastic, soft-touch rubber, and hardened steel across all of its components. The magnetic hex chuck is a standard quarter-inch, meaning that you should have wide compatibility with other bits that you might have lying around in the house, so long as they're magnetic. But with as many bits as you get in this kit, you might as well throw away the old bits to make way for the new, ultra-hard bits rated at 60HRC that come with this bundle. 25-piece Electronic Screwdriver Set: was $49.99 now $28.49 This Hoto magnetic electronic screwdriver is powered by a 1,500 mAh battery, allowing you to drive over 1,000 screws on a single USB-C charge. View Deal The screwdriver charges over a single USB-C port and also boasts features such as a three-stage setting for torque, making it perfectly suited to PC hardware builds, building furniture, or general household projects all year round. The electric motor spins at up to 220 RPM and weighs just 250g. You'll also get Hoto's magnetic case to keep the litter of bits contained and safe while it's not in use. For precision items like electronics, you might also want to take a look at a precision set from Hoto instead. But this kit is well-suited for most use cases you'll have, and will undoubtedly be a welcome addition to your toolset. title: These are the best gaming laptop deals we've found this Black Friday to suit all budgets

content: Getting a gaming laptop this Black Friday doesn't have to be a hassle. In case you're after the best deals that we've found thus far across a range of configurations, in addition to explanations of why these models in particular should be on your radar. Getting a gaming laptop is pretty tough — different systems can tout similar specs, but in reality, their performance can vary wildly. This is down to different power ratings across mobile GPUs, which can muddy the waters when you're looking on storefronts. It's often obfuscated in listings or omitted entirely. So we're here to cut through the noise and nonsense to bring you our picks of the best deals we've found thus far. We also have our Black Friday Gaming Laptop Deals Live Blog in action, so check that out if you want more options. Our top pick for most people: Asus ROG Strix G16 (RTX 5070 Ti, 115W) ROG Strix G16 (RTX 5070 Ti / Ryzen 9 8940HX): was $2299.99 now $1749.99 The Asus ROG Strix G16 comes with a 16-inch screen, with an 1900 x 1200 pixel resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, and refresh and response rates of 165Hz and 3ms, respectively. Hardware inside this gaming laptop includes Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5070 Ti laptop GPU, an AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX processor, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD for storage. View Deal This Asus ROG Strix G16 gaming laptop offers a solid price-to-performance ratio and comes with AMD's Ryzen 9 8940HX CPU, sporting 16 cores and 32 threads. Packing in the gaming punch is the included RTX 5070 Ti 12GB, with GDDR7 memory and a total graphics power of 115W; this is the full-fat variant of the chip, and dynamic boost can also see this rise to up to 140W. When paired with a relatively modest screen resolution and display, it certainly bodes well for getting solid performance from modern titles. And you should be able to saturate the display's refresh rate when turning on features like Multi Frame Generation in single-player titles. One thing to keep in mind here is that the laptop does sacrifice display quality, and its CPU isn't on the latest Zen 5 architecture; it's based on AMD's Zen 4 Dragon Range refresh chips. But it's still mighty fast and should suit both gaming and productivity workloads. Alternative pick: MSI Vector 16 HX AI (RTX 5070 Ti, 115W) Vector 16 HX AI (RTX 5070 Ti / Core Ultra 7 255HX): was $1999 now $1599 Get a 16-inch gaming laptop with Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX, RTX 5070 Ti with 12GB of VRAM, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD. View Deal Coming in slightly cheaper than the above Asus ROG Strix system, this MSI Vector 16 HX AI laptop from Newegg offers much of the same specifications: right down to the TGP of the GPU. MSI's 5070 Ti mobile chip carries the same 115W TGP, in addition to the screen resolution. It also moves CPUs to Intel's 20-core, 20-thread Core Ultra 7 255HX, which is a newer architecture compared to the ROG Strix G16's Dragon Range offering. However, you get a lower screen refresh rate at 144Hz and half the storage included. It does trade blows effectively with the Asus model in many respects, though, including offering dual Thunderbolt 5 ports and a 2.5GbE port over the ROG Strix's 1GbE port. With the sizes of modern games, though, it's tough to outright tell you to run out and purchase a system with only 512 GB of storage, so this system remains our alternative pick for most people. Budget pick: MSI Crosshair 16 (RTX 5060, 115W) Crosshair 16 (RTX 5060 / Ryzen 7 8840HX): was $2099 now $1199 The MSI Crosshair sports a 16-inch, 240Hz display with a 2560 x 1600 resolution that's powered by an 115W max TGP Nvidia RTX 5060 graphics with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM. Other specs include an AMD Ryzen 7 8840HX processor, 16GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD. View Deal This MSI Crosshair 16 deal at Walmart sports a tricked-out 115W RTX 5060 GPU at its core, alongside a 12-core, 24-thread AMD Ryzen 7 8840HX Dragon Range CPU that can boost up to 5.1GHz. Sporting 1TB of NVMe storage and 16GB of DDR5 RAM, this more entry-level system can offer solid computing power while staying within a limited budget. Something that prospective buyers should watch out for is the display's resolution: you get a 16:10, 2560 x 1600 screen resolution and 240Hz refresh rate on this system, meaning that the laptop will likely struggle in modern titles, especially at high settings. Turning on upscaling tech like DLSS might help smooth things over somewhat, but given that you'll be doing things other than gaming on this laptop, it makes for a comfortable everyday system that offers a sharp display. Alternative budget pick: Lenovo Legion 5i (RTX 5060, 115W) Legion 5i Gaming Laptop (RTX 5060 / Core Ultra 7 245HX): was $1899.99 now $1199.99 Lenovo's Legion 5i sports a 15.3-inch, 3K display that's powered by an Intel Core 7 245HX processor, an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 graphics card, and 16GB of RAM. You get the same 115W RTX 5060 silicon as the MSI model above, but with an Intel Core 7 245HX, with 14 cores and 14 threads and a boost clock of up to 5.1GHz on the P-cores. You also get the same 16:10 aspect ratio and 2560 x 1600 resolution, but on a 165Hz OLED panel. If you care about getting the best contrast ratios and response time, this might be the pick for you, as saturating a 240Hz display with an RTX 5060 mobile variant will be a pretty tall task. However, this comes with the downside that you once again sacrifice the amount of storage available on the system here, with only 512GB available here. High-end pick: HP Omen Max 16 (RTX 5080, 150W) Omen Max 16 (RTX 5080 / Ryzen AI 9 HX 375): was $3899 now $2899.99 Get an HP Omen Max laptop with an RTX 5080 GPU, Ryzen 9 HX 375, a 1TB SSD, and 32GB of RAM, all packed into a 16-inch chassis with a 2560 x 1600 240Hz display. With that said, you get 1TB of storage here, which is slightly disappointing, but given how NAND pricing is going, it's par for the course right now. The difference between the Omen 16 Max and this Gigabyte model is that this particular RTX 5080 has a lower TGP of 115W, but maintains the same amount of VRAM. Premium pick: HyperX Omen MAX 16 (RTX 5090 / 175W) Omen Max 16 (RTX 5090 / Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus ): was $4999.99 now $3799.99 Get an HP Omen Max laptop with an RTX 5090 GPU, a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus CPU, a 2TB SSD, and 32GB of RAM, all packed into a 16-inch chassis with a 2560 x 1600 240Hz OLED display. Sporting an RTX 5090 GPU with 24GB of GDDR7 memory, paired with Intel's Core Ultra 290 HX Plus, with a total of 24 cores and 24 threads (8 P-Cores, 16 E-Cores), and a boost clock of up to 5.5GHz, this monstrous system is paired with 32GB of DDR5-6400 memory and 2TB of PCIe Gen 5 storage. If you're spending north of $3,000 on a laptop, this should be it. Alternative premium pick: Asus ROG Strix Scar (RTX 5090 / 175W) ROG Strix Scar 16 - 2025 (RTX 5090, Core Ultra 9 275HX): was $4499.99 now $4149.99 Get a great deal on this flagship-class ROG Strix Scar 16 gaming laptop from Amazon. You get the Core Ultra 9 275HX 8p/16e (24 threads) processor, 32GB dual-channel DDR5-5600 RAM, 2TB M.2 PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD, a 16-inch Mini-LED display (2560x1600) with a fast 240 Hz refresh rate, and the pièce de résistance: a dedicated RTX 5090 24GB laptop GPU. You'll be able to play most games at high frame rates or even run your own local AI models. View Deal At MSRP pricing, the ROG Strix Scar is a better buy every other day. But given that it's black friday, the value offered by the HP Omen Max 16 slightly edges out this equally performant ROG Strix Scar 16 deal at Newegg. Expect the same RTX 5090 laptop GPU with 24GB of GDDR7 memory, but swap in an Intel Core Ultra 275HX with a total of 24 cores and 24 threads with 8 P-Cores and 16 E-Cores with boost clocks of up to 5.4GHz. Additionally, this system offers slower DDR5-5600 memory and slower storage, running at PCIe 4.0 speeds. However, you do get dual Thunderbolt 5 ports, here, and a matte finish on the display. It's still an incredible laptop by all rights, however HP's option edges things out on value, and spec-wise. title: Best Black Friday Gaming PC Deals live
summary: The very best pre-built gaming PC deals you can buy on Black Friday.
content: Gaming PCs are some of the most popular deals this Black Friday, because they're a more economical way to get into PC gaming now that component prices have gone up. Large vendors and OEMs are more insulated from price hikes on SSDs, RAM, and GPUs, and many have existing stock of quality parts. Therefore, buying a gaming PC is often now cheaper than building one by yourself. That's because 32GB of RAM now costs just over $400, while a 1TB SSD is around $250 at standard market prices. An RTX 5090 is basically impossible to buy, while an RTX 5080 will set you back $2,000. So if you were to buy an RTX 5080 gaming PC, the GPU alone is worth $2,000, before you've added any other parts. We're tracking all the best prices on gaming PCs at Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Newegg, using our hands-on testing, reviews, benchmark data, and price tracking to recommend the best deals. We have our live list below, but you can also check our full list of Black Friday Gaming PC Deals here . title: Handy TP-Link 5-port gigabit ethernet switch returns to all-time low of $8 at Amazon — perfect for homelabbers, office setups and IoT networking
summary: The TP-Link LS1005G Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch is back down to its lowest-ever price at just $7.99 on Amazon as a part of their Black Friday sale. At over 53% off, an unmanaged switch buys you freedom and, crucially, more Ethernet ports to play around with.
content: If you're looking at wiring up your home or figuring out your entire networking situation, nothing ever beats being plugged into an Ethernet port. The TP-Link LS1005G Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch is back down to its lowest-ever price at just $7.99 on Amazon as a part of their Black Friday sale. At over 53% off, an unmanaged switch buys you freedom and, crucially, more Ethernet ports to play around with. This device is ideal for those looking to connect essential devices via Ethernet, like networked cameras, an office full of electronics, or a multi-system homelab setup. Check out the TP-Link Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch on Amazon When the switch is this cheap, it's difficult to overstate how useful it could be if you're a resident tinkerer like any of us on the Tom's Hardware staff team. Each port can deliver full gigabit speeds across a 10Gbps backplane on the switch. That means if you're running a rapid setup, you'll still get gigabit-level speeds across all devices that are connected to this unit. It's also useful for those who have mesh networks, with only one single Ethernet port coming out of a satellite node. This unmanaged switch will give you access to more ports and more wired devices without the pitfalls of hooking things up over Wi-Fi, which can be prone to interference or latency. In this scenario, though, you're ideally looking at the satellite node running a wired backhaul across your network to maintain stability and avoid pitfalls like packet loss. Back to a record low price The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices. View Deal Given the price, it's important to note what you don't get with an inexpensive, unmanaged switch such as this. You won't receive any Power over Ethernet on the LS1005G switch, so if your networked cameras rely on it, you should look elsewhere. Additionally, as it's unmanaged, you cannot... well... manage it. Strictly speaking, 1Gbps should be more than enough bandwidth for most at-home use cases, such as NAS systems or sending files across your network. But if you're regularly sending larger files and have the infrastructure to support it, then looking at a unit with faster ports might be worthwhile for you, but if you don't think you'll hit the gigabit ceiling often, it's a perfect set-and-forget device. In particular, for the gamers among you, gigabit ports will be more than stable enough to support online gaming, even in titles that demand no packet loss, like online Rollback netcode in competitive fighting games like Street Fighter 6 and Fatal Fury: City of the Wolves . Remember, sustaining the harmony of a wired network does have its benefits! At under $8 on Amazon, TP-Link's unmanaged switch fits a huge variety of use cases and is also just handy to keep around, in case you'll need one later down the line. title: Get a perfect Alienware 4K OLED 32" display with RGB subpixels for $150 off
summary: Get a perfect Alienware AW3226Q 4K OLED 32" display with RGB subpixels for $549.99, or $150 off — 165 Hz refresh rate, 1000-nits HDR, and Dolby Vision support
content: Usually, buying a monitor involves some sort of compromise: maybe it's not the brightest, or the refresh rate is low, or the text is blurry, etc. How about one that is essentially pitch-perfect? The Alienware AW3226Q, a 32" 4K OLED display with a 165 Hz refresh rate, RGB subpixel layout, and DisplayHDR 400 True Black and Dolby Vision certifications, can be yours for only $549.99 from the Dell store , or $150 off its regular price. Check out the Alienware AW3226Q 4K 32" OLED display for $549.99 at the Dell store. If you're keeping track of features and thinking that this monitor looks about perfect, you're absolutely correct. A resolution of 3840x2160 at 32" is about perfect for a balance between perceptual sharpness and graphics card load in gaming — plus, while ultra-wide displays are excellent for gaming, their curved nature doesn't quite lend itself as well to productivity tasks. AW3226Q: was $699.99 now $549.99 The Alienware is a sharp, colorful OLED display with 4K resolution, 165 Hz refresh rate, and Dolby Vision support. View Deal Make no mistake, though: this isn't a "work monitor." First off, the 165 Hz refresh rate is supported by Nvidia G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro compatibility for smooth motion in games, and the peak HDR brightness is 1000 nits, letting you enjoy gorgeous vistas with natural highlights and sun — like, say, in STALKER 2 , at least before a mutant chews your face off. As with most any OLED panel, the pixel response time is effectively zero, making for a blur-free experience, and the color gamut covers 99% of the DCI-P3 color space. The pure RGB subpixel layout is worth expanding on, with good reason — most forms of anti-aliasing, namely but not only for text in Windows, assume left-to-right RGB for each color component. Until relatively recently, OLED monitors had acceptable-to-poor text rendering, because they used unorthodox layouts like RGWB or RGBW pixel arrangements. Meanwhile, this one? content: We've shown you our selection of gaming laptops and PCs, but the sounds of explosions and dulcet tones of soundtracks deserve a lot better than some dollar-store earbuds you've had since you were a kid. Additionally, when you want some quiet time for yourself, those earbuds won't do you much good. To properly enjoy some aural bliss along with peace and quiet, we suggest the Sony WH-1000XM5 wireless headset, which can be obtained for only $169.99 from Best Buy , or 23% off its regular $219.99. Check out the Sony WH-1000XM5 at Best Buy for only $169.99 . The Sony XM line of headsets is known for its top-notch active noise cancellation (ANC), and I can attest to that as the proud owner of the XM4s. This later model has a much slimmer headband and improved noise control. As with other ANC sets, it's an over-ear, closed-back design that insulates you from the world outside. The driver units have 30-mm drivers backed by light and efficient neodymium magnets, with a carbon fiber composite dome. The Sony XM line of headsets is known for its top-notch active noise cancellation (ANC), and the WH-1000XM5s deliver on front, along with top-notch audio quality, support for lossless codecs, and a hardware equalizer. title: Kioxia's 3rd-gen XL-Flash hits Optane-class 3-microsecond read latency with 70% higher density
summary: Kioxia showed an XL-Flash Generation 3 prototype at KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo and named the upcoming GP2 SSD as its first product.
content: The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its new XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it. The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a new memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane , which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance. (Image credit: Kioxia) The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed. Kioxia XL-Flash generations vs. BiCS8 TLC Year Cells Die Read latency Gen 1 2019 SLC 128Gb under 5 µs Gen 2 2022 SLC or MLC 128Gb / 256Gb under 5 µs (SLC), under 10 µs (MLC) Gen 3 2026 prototype SLC (reported) 128Gb (reported) 3 µs (average) BiCS8 TLC 2023 TLC 1Tb 40 µs XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for new data. The newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count. The GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the new flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O . Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage. Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate. These drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first showed the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year . Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level , due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work. (Image credit: Kioxia) While the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia announced its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

title: This clever $11 external PC power switch lets you boot your rig without reaching under your desk
summary: This $11 desk gadget means you don't have to bend down to turn your PC on or off. It's a must-buy option for anyone with a gaming PC under their desk.
content: You've bought the big stuff: the SSDs, the RAM, the graphics card. Those are the obvious Black Friday deals for a PC gamer, but this is the perfect opportunity to step back and look at the gadgets and tools that you wouldn't normally think about, or even know about. That's where this SinLoon external power button comes in, on sale for just $11.19 . We'd normally run through all of the big, important specs here, but we don't really need to do that here because, well, there isn't any. You're buying an external power button. It connects to your PC. It turns it off, it turns it on, it restarts it (if you want it to). It has a two-meter cable that you can use to connect it to your PC, either using your PC's front panel with the supplied splitter or directly to your motherboard. It's also, by design, got a pair of mechanical keyboard keys: these'll be the ones you press to turn your rig on or off. ● Check out this deal at Amazon External Power Button for Desktop PC: was $13.99 now $11.19 This gaming-friendly external power button has a 2-meter (78.74 inch) cable, along with a splitter that lets you connect both buttons to your case's front panel buttons. It also includes adhesive pads and zip-ties. View Deal Simple enough, then, but that's not to downplay what you're getting here, or how it's been made. Mechanical keyboard keys are an interesting choice, because they look like they've been plucked straight from a top-spec gaming keyboard, especially with the RGB lighting underneath. It's a showstopper by design. SinLoon could have just gone for a big, round button, but by going for a design that uses mechanical keyboard keys, they're making sure this button has longevity. That's why SinLoon reckons these keys are good for no less than five million keystrokes. You can switch your PC on or off five million times before this board wears out. That's a lot of restarts. The two keys themselves sit in a smooth, black plastic case. The wiring is black, too, and sheathed (mostly) in glossy plastic, extending from the back. It does eventually split into different colored cables, though, each labeled so you know their purpose and where you'll need to connect them. While you will need to open up your PC to get this installed, it's an easy enough process, as long as your case lets you get close to your PC's front panel headers. PC builders won't have much trouble with this, as you've probably already dealt with these cables when you've hooked it up to your motherboard. It's the same process for these cables, and it comes with connectors to handle the power and disk access LEDs, too. You don't have to sacrifice your PC's power buttons, either. This SinLoon power button comes with a 1-to-2 splitter, a physical adapter that lets you connect these cables alongside the cables handling your PC's power and reset buttons. It's a physical adapter, so if the pinout doesn't quite match up, you can just move the header cables around until it works. You can also totally bypass your PC's power button, if you prefer, by just connecting the cables up to your motherboard without the splitter. You may not need this, but for $11, it's the ultimate buy for a techie's desk. You might not have ever thought about a desktop power button, but look: it's cool, and it's useful. It's not just a pointless desk ornament, but a practical tool that'll help you turn your rig on or off. If you've got your PC in a place that's difficult to reach, it solves an obvious problem, too. You'll also find it useful if you're a maker or builder. For instance, open test rigs (like the ones we use at Tom's Hardware ) might not have a case, just a motherboard on a desk with a bunch of parts attached. Rather than shorting the header pins to start your rig (not the best idea), you can attach this SinLoon button instead to make the whole process safer and easier. The $11.19 sale price for this SinLoon external power button is cheap enough to make it easy to justify. It'll quickly improve a quality-of-life issue at your desk and it'll look cool doing it, especially if you've already got RGB peripherals on your desk to match. Whether it's for yourself or as a gift for a PC builder in your life, grab this cool desk item on sale while the discount lasts. title: Activists enter third day of hunger strike outside Anthropic's San Francisco HQ over recursive AI self-improvement
summary: Anti-RSI activists go into third day of hunger strike at Anthropic offices — acceleration of AI development creates growing concerns
content: The AI market and its developments have continually garnered opposition from several areas of society, to the point where protests are now frequent. On the day of Anthropic's IPO, Nov. 19, there were protests in multiple locations . As of right now, there's a fellow by the name of Elliot Callender on his third day of hunger strike in front of Anthropic's San Francisco offices, protesting against the company's use of RSI, or AI Recursive Self-Improvement. For now, he seems gung-ho about the effectiveness of his hunger strike, remarking that "It would be bad press for Anthropic if I had to go 40+ days to pressure them," and noted that he intends to protest with OpenAI once he's done with Anthropic. He also urges California residents to ring up Governor Gavin Newsom and request a legislative session on the topic of RSI. Callender just had a fellow protester join him now, too, though they might have a hard road ahead changing the hearts of CEOs who believe your ownership of RAM is a bad thing , and that immersive video games would be excellent entertainment for those unemployed due to AI. RSI is an AI training method wherein a model is put to work to improve itself repeatedly in a test-feedback-improve loop, purportedly making for much faster evolution compared to normal methods. It's a safe bet that most every frontier lab is using it, and Anthropic in particular has said that Claude wrote 90% of its own code back in September. Many AI opponents consider that the field is moving too fast , for several reasons. The first claim is that there's not enough time or oversight to ensure the proper testing and safety of the developed models. Others consider that the economic impact is too violent and coming in too fast and would broadly prefer a slowdown. Some also consider that reaching some sort of general intelligence (AGI) is feasible and see that as a doomsday scenario best left to cinematic productions. Proponents of RSI broadly coalesce around the fact that if one lab, or a nation's labs, stop using RSI, then someone else inevitably will — particularly but not only from nations with questionable human rights track records. The protesters' counter-argument is that countries need AI cooperation treaties, a point that Callender subscribes to: "they should stop doing RSI, put all of their money into lobbying for a bilateral AI treaty, and directly warn their users about their product." Such treaties are viewed with skepticism at best, considering how physically invisible model training is, requiring just data centers with the appropriate hardware. If the current U.S.-China-Nvidia situation surrounding high-end AI accelerators is any illustration, it's arguable if there's truly any international interest in controlling frontier AI development to begin with, much less choosing how quickly it's performed.

title: Beijing’s AI ambitions are under threat as models may fall behind by up to nine months versus competitors — Chinese AI labs are under heavy fire from export controls, maturing chip stacks and a distillation crackdown
summary: This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models.
content: This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months. Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time . In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported. These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips , and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another issue: tightened security against the distillation of AI models. Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information , this is an issue that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months. The current standings If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google, and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks. It's important to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains. With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them? China still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with users, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months. With devices like the RTX Spark , AMD's AI Halo , and more, users are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap. This is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official. The silicon transition Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts currently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s. If China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.

title: Nvidia agrees to $290 million settlement over 2018 crypto mining GPU sales
summary: Nvidia agrees to pay $290 million settlement for class action allegedly misleading investors that much of gaming GPU sales were actually driven by cryptocurrency mining demand.
content: Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit. Investors accused the company of misleading shareholders about how much of its gaming revenue was actually driven by the cryptocurrency mining boom in 2018. 2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017. Nvidia also sold the P106-100 that year, a dedicated cryptocurrency mining GPU with similar hardware to the GTX 1060, and it was attributed to OEM sales. Many gamers remember how scarce retail gaming GPUs were in those years, yet Huang stated in November 2017 that what cryptocurrency contributes is “small but not zero,” as highlighted in the Summary of Alleged False and Misleading Statements section of the March court filing . When the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales. The plaintiffs saw this strong correlation, seeing how cryptocurrency demand closely followed gaming GPU sales. The litigation states that Nvidia was “forced to partially reveal the truth on August 16, 2018, when it lowered their revenue guidance and acknowledged that ‘a great deal’ of cryptocurrency miners had bought GeForce Gaming GPUs.” Following the admissions, Nvidia’s stock price also fell 28.5% over two trading sessions. After the crash, Nvidia struggled with excess inventory, with CFO Colette Kress stating that “Gaming was short of expectations as post-crypto channel inventory took longer than expected to sell through,” painting a clearer picture of how much crypto impacted Nvidia’s sales, which were allegedly attributed to gaming sales. It’s unclear how much of those gaming sales were from cryptocurrency mining, but considering that an overwhelming amount of retail gaming GPUs were bought out by cryptocurrency miners, it’s reasonable to say it’s difficult to keep track of who purchased and for what purpose. In 2021, the district court dismissed the lawsuit, but part of the dismissal was reversed by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviving the lawsuit and allowing the securities fraud claims against Nvidia to proceed. Nvidia still denies wrongdoing, but has decided to settle, agreeing with the plaintiffs to pay $290 million in September, according to the Tuesday court filing .

title: AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let attackers brute-force BitLocker PINs on millions of PCs
summary: AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let hacks let malfeasants guess Bitlocker PINs on millions of machines — brute-forcing a six-digit PIN takes 20 days instead of 19 years, at most.
content: Former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today. Firmware-backed drive encryption setups like Windows' BitLocker are meant to protect against someone stealing your laptop or desktop computer. Prospective thieves would have a hard time guessing your PIN, as they'll eventually have to wait 10 minutes for each attempt. That is, unless your machine uses a modern AMD CPU or relies on Winbond's SPI flash — in which case your data may be open for inspection in a few days, or even hours, as researchers from Technische Universität Berlin found out . The paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the big three. All focus on having a way to brute-force an encrypted drive's password in a matter of days/hours rather than years. Physical access is required for the attacks, but hardware theft is precisely the scenario that disk encryption is meant to protect against. An attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts. On Intel- and AMD-based PCs using the fTPM for security — nearly all modern x86 consumer machines — this counter is stored encrypted in an SPI flash chip on the motherboard. Standard procedure is to allow for 32 attempts in succession, then force the machine to wait 10 minutes for each additional one, resulting in many years for unlocking a short PIN — 19 years for a six-digit numerical PIN, under normal conditions. We should note the attacks likely extend to other fTPM-based disk encryption mechanisms, not just BitLocker. While encryption keys can be alphanumeric, Microsoft Windows does default to using a numeric PIN for sign-in, and most users don't use long ones. First up: machines based on Winbond's RPMC-enabled SPI flash (variant with rollback protection), used by many OEMs across both Intel and AMD platforms. Although it's hard to pin down the number of affected machines, the paper claims Winbond has roughly a 25% market share for SPI flash — so, potentially millions of machines. With a simple voltage glitch, the researchers made the chip reveal the HMAC key, the datum that signs commands when the TPM and the SPI chip talk to each other. With the HMAC in hand, the thief places a low-cost interposer board in front of the SPI chip to impersonate it. On a failed unlock, the computer will request a counter increase and get a confirmation, when in reality nothing happened — allowing for repeat attempts as fast as Windows lets them, at five per reboot. There is no fix for this vulnerability other than replacing the SPI chip with one that doesn't contain the bug. The team glitched two specific Winbond chip models, but they theorize the issue extends further into the maker's lineup, as the flaw allegedly lies with the RPMC engine design. Flash chips from other firms in the test were not affected to the same extent. As for AMD machines, the situation is both worse and better, with two related vulnerabilities. The team verified at least one of the two attacks across AMD machines from Zen 2 up to an AI 5 330 laptop. They theorize that considering the mechanisms, all contemporary AMD setups may be vulnerable, at least for standard consumer hardware using fTPM. That's multiple millions of machines potentially at risk, on the low side. The first is simple enough. On the tested machines whose SPI flash didn't use RPMC — rollback protection — you can just make a copy of the SPI flash's contents when the counter is low, and just flash it again once you've used up your free tries. Bad enough, yes, but the second vulnerability should elicit facepalms from security architects. According to the paper, AMD's firmware controller for non-volatile storage — the bit that talks to the SPI flash — does not verify that the failed-attempt counter increase actually took place. It'll just issue the order to +1 it and be done, opening the avenue for an attacker to simply intercept that order (again, with a cheap board) and ignore it without even needing HMAC keys, so the counter never changes. The latter vulnerability should be fixable via a firmware update, almost certainly via AMD's AGESA software. The problem is one of practicality: in the past, updating AGESA on client hardware meant that every OEM had to create fresh BIOSes for affected machines, many of which are assuredly out of their support window. Anyone who's lived through the Spectre and Meltdown days knows how hard it is in practice, as OEMs are exceedingly slow to publish updates, and have a distaste for providing fixes for hardware that's more than a few years old. The researchers contacted every company involved in their tests, informing them of their findings, but sadly "none of them has committed to fixing the root-cause vulnerabilities" — at least, as of this writing, only Microsoft announced a policy change recommending users enter six-digit PINs instead of the current four during setup.

title: Texas lifts freeze on 1,800+ data center projects in Greg Abbott U-turn
summary: After pausing the approval of new data center building permits in August, Texas has now reversed the decision and has once again begun approving applications as builders rush to get the go-ahead before Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa's January arrival.
content: After slamming the brakes on more than 1,800 data center projects in August, Texas has once again started approving them following a new directive from outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott's office. The move came after the same office also paused the approval of permits, saying that Abbot's "top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life” amid concerns over the amount of power new data centers would require. At the time, the move meant that 474 gigawatts of new power requests became subject to the moratorium. But with Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa's January arrival edging ever closer, Abbott has done a 180-degree pivot, with the FT reporting that data center builders are rushing to get their approvals in before the new governor arrives. Hinojosa has already pledged to rein in new data center construction. As recently as October, Texas suspended a further 17 data center construction permits and shut down an automated portal that was found to still be approving new permits. That system will surely be switched back on now that Abbott's office has confirmed that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which is in charge of the state’s electrical grid, has finished gathering the information that it needed on how data centers affect local communities. But even with ERCOT's investigation complete, the processing of new power requests isn't one that is expected to happen quickly. With that in mind, some developers have already taken matters into their own hands, choosing to build their own power centers to reduce or eliminate their reliance on the local grid. The region's large gas supplies are helping this effort, as is what is considered to be a "lax" regulatory environment. This all means that the possibility of using gas turbines to power new data centers is a viable one, although some are looking beyond traditional gas-powered options. In Mississippi, Elon Musk's xAI installed eight converted jet engines to power its data center, despite the known health risks posed by their use. While it remains to be seen what impact the arrival of incoming Governor Hinojosa will have on data centers in the area, there's little doubt that they will be a hot topic. Locals continue to be concerned about the environmental impact these facilities have, while increased costs associated with powering their own homes are another issue. Texas isn't alone in facing these problems, with New York announcing a year-long ban on data center projects larger than 50 megawatts that came into force earlier this year. In Northern Virginia, Amazon abandoned plans to build four new data centers after public outcry. The land will now be used for housing instead.

title: Ukrainian 11th-grader builds AI-powered, GPS-free drone autopilot to beat frontline jamming
summary: Yaroslav Sheiko's innovation allows drones to fly accurately even if they don't have a GPS signal or encounter GPS jamming.
content: An 11th-grade student has received “The Future of Ukraine” from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for multiple technical achievements. According to Poltava Wave , Yaroslav Sheiko, a student from Poltava, located about 190 miles to the west of Kyiv, built an AI-powered drone autopilot system, allowing uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) to reach their destination without relying on GPS signals, and an optical-electronic stabilization system. This award is just the latest among Sheiko’s achievements. The 11th-grader has already received two presidential scholarships for his academic performance and contributions to science, as well as getting the top award twice in nationwide competitions held by Ukraine’s Junior Academy of Sciences. He has also competed internationally, receiving a gold medal in the INOVA 2025 International Inventions Show and a silver medal in the 2025 Hackathon. Even though Ukraine relies on military assistance from its allies, it’s also working on homegrown technologies to improve its drone capabilities. Some of these breakthroughs include equipping its grounded fleet of U.S.-made Puma reconnaissance drones with domestic anti-jamming systems and using a network of “flying modems” to increase the range of its attack drones without having to use unreliable Starlink connections . It was the first to use a heavy-lift UAV to evacuate a wounded soldier from a minefield and conduct a 12-hour, 1,500-mile strategic drone strike on Russian targets. The country is also working on anti-drone systems, like using old Android phones as an acoustic sensor network as an early warning system to spot drones and shooting down Russian jet drones using a cheap, high-powered laser air defense system. The widespread use of drones in Ukraine also meant that other countries have started developing their own drone and anti-drone technologies and forces. China has revealed a 200-strong AI drone swarm controlled by a single soldier using an “intelligent algorithm,” while Japan is working on an ultra-cheap cardboard drone swarm that only costs $2,000 per unit. The UK is also deploying the DragonFire anti-drone laser on Royal Navy destroyers by 2027. As for the U.S., it’s training military units on both land and sea to 3D-print combat-ready drones , assemble and maintain units in-house, and even adapt them depending on the mission at hand. Ukraine has not detailed how Sheiko’s inventions work, but what’s more important is that these innovations are crucial to Ukraine’s war effort, especially with the amount of jamming and electronic warfare present on the front lines. More than that, his skill and talent may prove to be a crucial asset for Ukraine and its defense industry, especially as Russia’s invasion has already been ongoing for 12 years, with a full-scale conflict going on since 2022.

title: China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes
summary: AI hardware bottlenecks are expanding beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them. As AI servers like Rubin Ultra push PCB layers toward 78 layers using denser laminates, drill bits are wearing out 10 times faster than normal, while high-speed signalling stretches the demand for smooth copper foil.
content: Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors , as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require. More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion plans in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is important because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials. It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components. More holes, fewer uses PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs. But that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities , the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process. As well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. New grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. The increasingly common use of harder laminates is resulting in the bits being consumed more quickly. That’s good news for those making drill bits: HSBC forecasts global demand growing 55% a year in the coming three years. And as with many parts of the AI revolution, the voracious appetite of the sector means that supplies can’t keep up. Even with manufacturers increasing production, the bank forecasts a 24% supply shortfall in PCB drill bits in 2027. That could push the world towards Chinese suppliers, right as the west is trying to wean itself off a dependency on the country for rare earths and other elements necessary to make GPUs. Guangdong Dtech, based in China, is the world’s largest PCB drill bit maker by volume. Around three in every 10 drill bits made in 2025 come from the company, with its monthly capacity potentially climbing from 160 million bits in June to more than 235 million by year-end. Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers are still dominant at the premium end of the market, according to consultancy Frost & Sullivan, though Chinese manufacturers are trying to close that gap. In its 2026 interim results , Dtech reported that it had begun mass-producing drill bits with aspect ratios exceeding 40:1, while developing techniques for producing bits exceeding 60:1. Its newer diamond-coated tools for particularly tough M9+ board materials have also entered small-scale use. China calling It’s not just in drill bits that China has a chokehold. Another Chinese manufacturer, Defu Technology, has historically been a key supplier of copper foil for lithium-ion batteries, but is increasingly changing its manufacturing processes to try and capitalise on the AI boom. “AI server PCB/CCL upgrades require smoother HVLP copper foil to reduce high-speed signal loss,” writes Avery Chan, a JP Morgan analyst. HVLP stands for hyper-very-low-profile copper foil, and its manufacturers must make the surface smooth enough to minimise signal loss while making sure it can still stick to the insulating material it is attached to. The business has historically been dominated by suppliers outside mainland China, with Japan’s Mitsui Kinzoku and Furukawa Electric, and Taiwan’s Co-Tech, holding more than 60% of global HVLP supply in 2025. Defu is trying to break in to disrupt that, with the firm shipping around 700 tonnes of HVLP foil in September, including more than 180 tonnes of HVLP4. JP Morgan’s Chan forecasts a shortage of qualified HVLP4 supply of around 700 tonnes a month in 2026, rising to 1,200 tonnes in 2027. Defu plans to add 50,000 tonnes of annual high-end PCB foil capacity over 2027 and 2028. But all the foil it creates will have to get past stringent testing. Testing chips Even before finished chips reach a server, they must be tested using specialist probe cards and sockets, which themselves rely on sophisticated PCBs of a type not found in a server but just used to check whether the chips work. “PCB is becoming the bottleneck and the value-add in probe cards,” wrote JP Morgan analyst Jerry Tsai. Because of that, China is focusing attention there, too. In September, its Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and National Development and Reform Commission published a five-year plan calling for advances in high-frequency, high-speed and densely layered PCBs, alongside copper-clad laminates, low-profile copper foil and specialist manufacturing equipment. But China won’t see the benefits of building new factories immediately. Producing the most sophisticated PCBs requires experience, specialist equipment and the ability to manufacture complex designs consistently at scale. Tsai warned that “the learning curve is measured in years, rather than quarters.”

title: TSMC gives a sneap peak at AI Design Kit: Agentic AI with foundry expertise
summary: TSMC brings agentic AI to chip design as A14 design rule count hits 3.6X that of N5 while customers demand 33% shorter development cycle.
content: The semiconductor industry is in a paradoxical situation these days. On the one hand, AI drives demand for the leading-edge nodes from both established players and new entrants, with everyone trying to accelerate the development cycle. On the other hand, leading-edge nodes become more complex, which increases entry barriers and stretches design cycles. While the challenge seems to be insoluble, it looks like TSMC has found a solution. (Image credit: TSMC) At its 2026 Europe OIP Ecosystem Workshop in Munich, TSMC this week unveiled its AI Design Kit (ADK), a collection of process-specific technical information, implementation guidelines, and design methodologies that enables AI agents to automate and optimize chip development flows. The ADK complements the foundry's traditional process design kits (PDKs) and enables AI agents to use TSMC's process-specific expertise, knowledge of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, and customers' proprietary design methodologies to automate physical implementation and optimization of chips. Ultimately, the initiative aims to reduce development cycles, improve design productivity, and simplify adoption of TSMC's advanced process technologies. "The ADK complements our traditional PDK, and it brings in capabilities to augment the EDA and other design flows," said Aveek Sarkar, Head of Ecosystem and Alliance Management at TSMC. "Our goal with these agentic flows is to bring in the technology-specific learning we have at TSMC and layer that with your orchestration layer, with your design expertise, and to support the next generation of EDA or design flows and methodologies that you have." Why AI? While every new fabrication process from TSMC offers advantages in terms of power, performance, and area (PPA), it also considerably increases design complexity. Compared to TSMC's N5-derived manufacturing technologies (including various N4 nodes), the number of design rules has increased by 2.3X with N3P, 3.1X with N2P, and 3.6X with A14 (the first node to be supported by the ADK). Meanwhile, the number of available standard library cells has increased by 2.8X, 5X, and 4.6X, respectively. Add to that a greater number of metallization stack options and plenty of EDA tool settings, and the number of possible design configurations becomes massive. As a result, conventional design optimization methodologies approach their productivity limits, according to TSMC. At the same time, some of TSMC's customers want to reduce their chip development cycles from 18 months to 12 months, Sarkar said. Technology N5/N4P N3P N2P NanoFlex A14 NanoFlex Pro Library HD, HP HD, HP, UHP HD, HP, UHP + Boost Cells HD, HP + Boost Cells Cell Count 1.0x 2.8x 5.0x 4.6x Rule Count 1.0x 2.3x 3.1x 3.6x Usage of agentic AI could help chip developers to explore more design configurations within shorter timeframes, achieve more favorable PPA results from advanced process technologies, and potentially improve manufacturability and yields by implementing more extensive physical design optimization. Furthermore, it could reduce the amount of engineering work required to adopt a new fabrication process for a new design. "AI is bringing a significant benefit: faster design cycles, more verification coverage, faster time to closure," Sarkar said. Do physical implementation faster TSMC's early-phase AI Design Kit incorporates process-specific information, such as metal pitches, standard cell heights, routing track patterns, library cell naming conventions, and implementation guidelines, according to slides demonstrated at the event. (Image credit: TSMC) With the ADK, EDA agents — such as Cadence's InnoStack or Synopsys's Implementation Agent — can use a simple natural-language prompt and a large language model (LLM) to automatically generate a qualified automatic placement and routing (APR) reference flow for TSMC's A14 process technology. Such a flow includes project setup, library cell usage, placement and routing optimization, routing track and power grid creation, and wide-wire configuration. Traditionally, engineers could spend weeks on preparation of such scripts, but now APR scripts could be prepped with a natural language prompt, though TSMC did not disclose the actual time it takes to prep them (probably because it depends on design complexity and goals). "Instead of spending weeks preparing APR scripts, EDA agents can take a simple prompt from users and the TSMC ADK and use a generative model to deliver a qualified APR reference flow," a spokesperson from TSMC said at the stage. For more sophisticated design tasks, TSMC proposes an orchestration agent that resides at the customer's site and combines three sources of knowledge with clear ownership: Proprietary in-house design know-how, constraints, guidelines, and customized flow; Specialized EDA agents that know how to use EDA tools and their capabilities; TSMC's ADK that provides design reference package and technology-specific information on top of what EDA agent and tools know. The orchestrator coordinates agents responsible for design diagnostics, power grid implementation, timing closure, design rule checks, and congestion mitigation. These agents analyze EDA tool output and automatically adjust parameters for subsequent iterations across floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, sign-off, and engineering change orders (ECOs). Such a methodology enables continuous design optimization 24/7 with less human intervention. "The orchestrator then directs these agents to analyze the output of EDA tools and automatically adjust the settings for the next iteration across floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, sign-off, and ECO," the spokesman said. "This agentic AI flow drives the iterative design process 24/7, minimizing the turnaround time and maximizing productivity." Complement, not replace For now, TSMC's ADK primarily addresses physical implementation rather than chip architecture or logic design. The company has not demonstrated an autonomous design flow that takes a chip from an architectural specification to tape-out without human intervention. Nor has TSMC disclosed quantified PPA improvements, actual reductions in development cycles, or a commercial availability timeframe for its ADK. It is noteworthy that TSMC's ADK neither replaces conventional PDKs nor substitutes for advanced AI-enabled EDA software from Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, or other developers. Instead, it provides process-specific knowledge that enables AI agents to make more informed decisions, while the actual physical implementation, simulation, optimization, and verification tasks remain the domain of specialized EDA tools. Thus, chip developers cannot use the ADK independently of traditional EDA infrastructure. Strategic importance For TSMC, the ADK could accelerate adoption of its latest fabrication processes, as customers could adapt their design methodologies to new nodes faster. Smaller fabless chip developers could also gain access to sophisticated physical design methodologies without the need to develop expertise comparable to that of prominent chip developers entirely in-house. Meanwhile, EDA and IP providers could benefit from closer integration of their products into process-specific design flows, whereas contract chip designers could offer shorter development times for their customers without significant additional investments. There is also a potential customer lock-in aspect. While TSMC's proposed architecture preserves customers' ownership of proprietary design knowledge, extensive integration of foundry-specific physical design enablement collateral, EDA agents, and internal orchestration systems could make migration to another foundry harder and generally less likely as chipmakers get more accustomed to TSMC ADK (which is an exclusive capability for now and will remain an exclusive offering for a while). In effect, TSMC's competitive advantages will extend well beyond its process technologies, production capabilities, and conventional design ecosystem to include intelligence that emphasizes its customers' chip development methodologies.
